subject: Biology
title: Deforestation and Its Effects
description: One-minute skill: Deforestation and Its Effects.

hook.text: Every minute, an area of tropical forest the size of 30 soccer fields is destroyed.

buildup.text: Forests are cleared for cattle ranching, palm oil, soy farming, and logging.

discovery.text: Trees absorb CO₂. Cutting them down releases stored carbon and removes future absorption.

twist.text: Deforestation also displaces indigenous peoples who have lived sustainably in forests for centuries.

climax.text: Reducing deforestation is one of the fastest ways to slow climate change and protect biodiversity.

punchline.text: Forests are easier to protect than to regrow.

quiz.question: What is the main driver of tropical deforestation?
options: Agriculture, especially cattle and palm oil

details.summary: Deforestation destroys roughly 10 million hectares of forest annually, releasing stored carbon, destroying habitats, and degrading watersheds. Tropical deforestation alone accounts for about 10 percent of global carbon emissions and threatens half of Earth's terrestrial species.
details.whyItMatters: Forests regulate climate, cycle water, prevent erosion, and harbor most terrestrial biodiversity. Deforestation for agriculture and logging undermines all these services, affecting weather patterns and livelihoods far beyond the cleared areas.
takeaways: About 10 million hectares of forest are lost each year globally
Tropical deforestation contributes roughly 10 percent of carbon emissions
Forest loss fragments habitats isolating wildlife populations

faq.question: What is the main driver of deforestation worldwide?
faq.answer: Agriculture is the leading cause, particularly cattle ranching and soy production in South America and palm oil plantations in Southeast Asia. Subsistence farming, logging, and infrastructure development also contribute significantly.

faq.question: Can deforested areas recover?
faq.answer: Secondary forests can regrow on abandoned land, but they take decades to centuries to approach the biodiversity and carbon storage of old-growth forests. Heavily degraded soils may not support forest recovery without active restoration.
